paper_title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Omni-modal large language models (Omni LLMs) [5, 25, 32, 33] can jointly process text, audio, images, and video, integrating cross-modal cues to interpret multimodal inputs and reason over the evidence they provide. Audio-visual reasoning in video scenarios is particularly difficult because it requires models to connect and analyze auditory and visual signals simultaneously. This involves identifying relevant evidence in each modality and integrating cues from different moments, abilities that support applications such as sports event understanding and the analysis of films and television programs. With the rapid development of Omni LLMs, accurately and reliably evaluating the capabilities of existing Omni LLMs has become particularly important, and is of great significance for identifying model shortcomings and driving their development. Existing benchmarks for joint audio-visual reasoning [2, 14, 16, 22, 31, 36] cover everyday activities, real-world scenarios, and diverse tasks, providing valuable ways to assess Omni LLMs. However, our analysis reveals key limitation of dominant multiple-choice question (MCQ) evaluations: correct answer does not necessarily demonstrate joint use of audio and visual evidence. As illustrated in Fig. 1, some questions can be answered using single modality or even textual cues alone. This ambiguity has two sources. First, answer-only scoring cannot distinguish evidence-supported answers from lucky guesses. Second, question and answer-option design can introduce unimodal or logical (text) shortcuts. For example, the correct option may be inferred from common knowledge, audio-only input, or vision-only input. Quantitative visualizations from existing benchmarks are provided in the Appendix D.1. Together, these limitations motivate an evaluation protocol that requires models to identify the audio and visual evidence supporting each answer, enabling complete evaluation of the entire reasoning chain. Motivated by these observations, we introduce EvaOmni, an EVidence-grounded benchmark for Audio-visual reasoning. It comprises 392 videos and 1,027 question-answer pairs spanning 15 fine-grained capabilities at three levels of reasoning and evidence complexity: Level 1-Retrieval & Grounding requires locating relevant audio and visual evidence; Level 2-Basic Understanding requires interpreting and combining complementary cues; and Level 3-Complex Reasoning requires understanding with complex evidence distribution, or performing multi-step cross-modal reasoning. Experts need to annotate the audio and visual intervals supporting each answer, and models must return both an answer and its supporting intervals. This design both greatly reduces annotation errors and prevents models from using shortcuts when answering questions. To ensure question quality, we designed series of rigorous annotation procedures: systematic video selection, expert annotation, cross-checking, and model-assisted filtering. These procedures help reduce text and unimodal 2 Figure 2 Top: We designed series of rigorous annotation procedures to ensure the quality and reliability of EvaOmni questions. Bottom: An example of Grounded Annotation, where, building on MCQ, we require models to output the audio and visual evidence intervals supporting the answer, in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain and prevent blind guessing and shortcuts. shortcuts. Such procedures ensure the high quality and reliability of our questions. We also propose two new evaluation metrics: the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.), which measures the coverage of annotated evidence identified by the model, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.), which penalizes inaccurate temporal localization in either modality. Both incorporate answer correctness to comprehensively evaluate the models reasoning ability. Additional grounded metrics are reported in the Appendix D.2. We conduct systematic evaluation of EvaOmni, involving seven open-weight models and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs. The best-performing proprietary model, Gemini3.7-Flash, achieves 79.4% accuracy, 70.8% C.G., and 35.1% B.G. overall. The strongest open-weight model, MiMo-V2.5-310B-A15B, achieves 56.8% accuracy, 48.4% C.G., and 20.5% B.G. Gemini3.7-Flash leads by 22.6, 22.4, and 14.6 percentage points, respectively. Relative to Qwen3-Omni-Instruct-30B-A3B (25.2% accuracy, 4.0% C.G., and 0.4% B.G.), MiMo-V2.5-310B-A15B scores 2.3, 12.1, and 51.3 times as high on these metrics, respectively. Despite this progress, the strongest proprietary models remain well below the human reference in localization quality: Gemini3.7-Flash achieves 35.1% B.G., compared with 94.3% for human experts. These findings demonstrate the importance of grounded evaluation, which cannot be captured by previous MCQ-based benchmarks. We hope EvaOmni brings some new insights to the development of omni-modal models: future models should not only pursue correct answers but also be able to precisely localize the evidence supporting their answers, so that their conclusions can be verified against the audio-visual input. We have publicly released EvaOmni, including its data, annotations, and evaluation framework, to support reliable, interpretable, and hierarchical evaluation of audio-visual reasoning.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Omni LLMs. Omni LLMs process text, images, video, and audio, enabling cross-modal understanding and reasoning [6, 7, 17]. ImageBind [8] learned shared representations across text, audio, depth, and images; PandaGPT [21] connected such representations to an LLM; and NExT-GPT [29] extended omni-modal systems to image, audio, and video generation. GPT-4o [15] introduced streaming speech generation for natural interaction. The Gemini [4, 23, 24] and Qwen [25, 32, 33] families are leading proprietary and open-weight Omni LLMs, respectively, advancing cross-modal understanding and reasoning. SeedRealtime [1] further integrates audio, video, and text in full-duplex architecture for continuous scene understanding, interaction-timing awareness, and responsive behavior. Together, these systems mark shift toward joint reasoning and natural interaction. Benchmarks for Omni LLMs. Unlike benchmarks of individual image, audio, or video understanding [3, 20, 27, 28, 34, 35], Omni LLM benchmarks assess joint cross-modal reasoning. DailyOmni [36] covers everyday scenarios; WorldSense [14] emphasizes audio-visual understanding in real-world videos; and OmniVideoBench [16] requires reasoning over both modalities. Yet text and unimodal shortcuts can undermine answer-only scores, and existing benchmarks do not jointly score answer correctness and the localization of supporting audio-visual evidence. Another evaluation approach, Open-Ended, relies on judge models and is thus insufficiently objective and convenient. Therefore, the research community currently urgently needs an evaluation system that is objective, convenient, and rigorous.

sections.title: 3.1 Rethinking Audio-Visual Reasoning Benchmarks
sections.content: Before introducing EvaOmni, let us revisit the existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks. Table 1 compares seven representative benchmarks. In the shortcut-checks column, T/A/V/I/Tr denote text-, audio-, video-, image-, and transcript-based tests; denotes an unspecified unimodal test, dependency and logic check, and human shortcut review. In the taxonomy column, cat., dims., diff., and caps. denote categories, dimensions, difficulty tiers, and capabilities. OmniBench uses static images, while SocialOmni focuses on social interaction rather than video question answering. Most existing benchmarks use multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and score responses by answer correctness. This raises RQ1: Can answer-only MCQ accuracy establish whether correct answer is grounded in both audio and visual evidence? It cannot: the same credit is assigned to evidence-supported answers and unsupported correct choices. For four-option questions, uniform random guessing yields an expected accuracy of 25%, illustrating one way to obtain correct answers without using either modality. We found that considerable proportion of questions in existing benchmarks can still be answered correctly without complete audio-visual input. For example, in WorldSense, 14.4% of questions can be answered correctly by looking only at the question and options, 14.2% can be answered correctly by listening only to the audio, and 15.7% can be answered correctly by watching only the video. Note that this does not represent strict shortcut ratio (it depends on our test models), but it still indicates that many shortcut problems exist in existing benchmarks. These observations motivate RQ3: How can we build benchmark that retains the objectivity and convenience of MCQs while effectively and reliably evaluating model performance in audio-visual reasoning? sections.title: Introducing EvaOmni
sections.content: To address RQ3, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark for audio-visual reasoning. For each question, expert annotators identify the audio and visual intervals supporting the correct answer. At evaluation time, models must provide both an answer and timestamped evidence intervals for each modality. EvaOmni evaluates answer correctness together with evidence coverage and temporal grounding, thereby limiting the credit awarded to correct answers that lack matching evidence. Text-only, audio-only, and vision-only checks during question construction further reduce shortcut susceptibility, as described below. EvaOmni organizes 15 fine-grained capabilities into three levels of reasoning and evidence complexity: Level 1: Retrieval and Grounding. Tests temporal alignment, event binidng, and entity binding, such as identifying the speaker of an utterance or linking sound to its visible source. Level 2: Basic Understanding. Requires models to interpret and integrate complementary audio-visual cues to understand events, scene context, and their relationships. Level 3: Complex Reasoning. Tests long-range reasoning, multi-evidence chains, and multi-hop reasoning. These tasks require models to integrate evidence from different moments, perform multiple inference steps, or both. The three levels contain 3, 9, and 3 capabilities, respectively, as summarized in Fig. 4(a). The detailed capability distribution is provided in the Appendix A.5.

sections.title: 3.3 Data Collection
sections.content: To mitigate potential training data contamination, we collect recent videos from open platforms such as YouTube and Bilibili. The selected 112-minute videos span diverse real-world scenarios and contain informative visual events and audio cues. We exclude videos with hard-coded subtitles or prominent textual overlays to limit OCR-based shortcuts. Detailed selection and screening criteria are provided in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3.4 Annotation Pipeline
sections.content: Expert annotators construct questions requiring joint use of audio and visual information and mark the temporal evidence for each modality. Each sample then undergoes human cross-validation for capability alignment, evidence quality, and potential textual or unimodal shortcuts. Disputed pairs receive independent review by two additional experts and are discarded unless both approve them. Model-assisted screening under text-only, audio-only, and visual-only inputs identifies additional shortcuts; pairs flagged at this stage are revised and re-evaluated. Appendix provides the full annotation and quality-control procedure.

sections.title: 3.5 Evaluation Metrics
sections.content: EvaOmni adopts composite evaluation metric that simultaneously assesses models answer correctness and evidence localization ability. We primarily use answer accuracy (Acc.) as well as additional grounded metrics, which are introduced below. For each question, the model returns an answer and audio and visual evidence intervals specified by start and end timestamps. We report two grounded scores that combine the answer score (s = 1 for correct option and = 0 otherwise) with evidence localization quality: 5 Figure 4 Overview and statistics of EvaOmni. (a) Hierarchical capability taxonomy. (b) Video duration statistics. (c) Mean question and answer-option lengths in tokens by level. (d) Mean counts and durations of annotated audio and visual evidence segments. (e) Video type distribution. Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.). This metric measures how much annotated audio and visual evidence is covered by the predictions. Let audioI and visualI be the numbers of human-annotated audio and visual evidence segments that have positive-duration temporal overlap with at least one predicted segment in the same modality. Each annotated segment is counted at most once. Let audioall and visualall denote the total numbers of annotated segments in the respective modalities. We define C.G. = (cid:18) audioI audioall + visualI visualall (cid:19) . (1) C.G. averages the two modality-specific evidence hit rates and weights them by answer correctness. We interpret C.G. as lenient evidence hit-rate metric, not measure of precise temporal localization: any positive-duration overlap counts as hit, and overly broad predictions are not directly penalized for imprecise interval boundaries. Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.). Let IoUaudio and IoUvisual denote the temporal intersection over union between predicted and human-annotated evidence for the audio and visual modalities, respectively. For each modality, we first take the union of all predicted intervals and the union of all annotated intervals; their IoU is the duration of the intersection of these two sets divided by the duration of their union. We define B.G. = min(IoUaudio, IoUvisual) . (2) Taking the minimum makes B.G. sensitive to the less accurately localized modality: strong localization in one modality cannot compensate for poor localization in the other. Thus, C.G. measures broad evidence coverage, whereas B.G. requires accurate localization in both modalities. Additional grounded metrics are provided in Appendix D.2.

sections.title: 4.2 Experimental Settings
sections.content: We evaluate all 24 models on 1,027 question-answer pairs drawn from 392 videos, using the same prompt and preprocessed audio-visual content. Video frames are uniformly sampled at 1.0 FPS and resized so that their longer side is 480 pixels while preserving the aspect ratio. Open-weight models outside the MiMo family are evaluated on single server equipped with eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, using the inference frameworks and settings recommended in their model cards. The open-weight MiMo models and all proprietary models are evaluated through their providers official APIs. The prompt, input preprocessing procedures, and further evaluation details are provided in the Appendix.

sections.title: 4.3 Main Findings
sections.content: Table 2 reports performance across capability levels and overall, while Figure 6 compares two representative models with human performance. We summarize the key findings below. Overall Performance Analysis. (1) substantial gap remains between the strongest evaluated open-weight and proprietary models. MiMo-V2.5-310B-A15B achieves overall Acc., C.G., and B.G. scores of 56.8%, 48.4%, and 20.5%, respectively, whereas Gemini3.7-Flash reaches 79.4%, 70.8%, and 35.1%. The respective gaps of 22.6, 22.4, and 14.6 percentage points span answer correctness, evidence coverage, and precise dual-modal localization. (2) The gap to human experts is especially pronounced in precise grounding. Human experts achieve 96.8% Acc., 96.0% C.G., and 94.3% B.G., exceeding Gemini3.7-Flash by 17.4, 25.2, and 59.2 percentage points, respectively. The models 79.4% accuracy and 70.8% C.G. indicate strong answering performance and substantial evidence coverage, yet its 35.1% B.G. reveals persistent difficulty in precisely localizing evidence in both modalities. Although grounded scores also incorporate answer correctness, the much smaller decline from Acc. to B.G. for humans (2.5 points, versus 44.3 for Gemini3.7-Flash) highlights the remaining grounding challenge. (3) Grounding limitations are more severe among the four open-weight models with fewer than 100B total parameters. Their overall C.G. ranges from 0.8% to 12.6% and B.G. from 0.3% to 4.0%, compared with 30.4%70.8% and 10.0%35.1% for the proprietary models. For example, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B achieves 16.4% accuracy but only 0.8% C.G. and 0.3% B.G. Jointly requiring correct answers and grounded evidence thus exposes limitations that answer-only evaluation can obscure. These models leave substantial room for improvement in consistently satisfying both dual-modal localization and answer correctness. In Figure 5, we compare the rankings of five models. Model rankings by grounding score broadly follow those by Acc., although few shifts in position highlight differences in evidence localization among models with similar answer accuracy. Finding 1: Grounded evaluation shows that even leading models trail humans in evidence localization, while open-weight models under 100B parameters lag behind proprietary models in evidence perception and localization. Analysis Across Capability Levels. Answer accuracy decreases from Level 1 to Level 2 for 21 of the 24 models, but increases from Level 2 to Level 3 for 13 models. For example, Gemini3.7-Flash improves from 73.6% to 79.1% accuracy between Levels 2 and 3, while its C.G. drops from 65.3% to 49.1% and B.G. from 29.2% to 12.3%. This divergence is consistent with the design of Level 3, which emphasizes long-range reasoning, combinations of multiple evidence segments, and multi-hop inference. These tasks place greater demands on assembling and localizing supporting evidence, without necessarily producing monotonic decline in multiple-choice accuracy. One plausible explanation is that partial evidence can help eliminate distractors and narrow the candidate set, allowing model to select the correct answer without fully localizing the supporting evidence. Table 3 reports cost-efficiency calculations for 10 selected proprietary models. We calculate total costs from provider API prices under common setting of 1,027 requests, each with 10-minute audio-visual input. Cost efficiency is calculated separately using the Overall Acc., C.G., and B.G. in Table 2: for total cost C, request count , and percentage score s, the corresponding cost efficiency is C/(N s/100). This gives the USD cost per unit of accumulated normalized score; lower values indicate better efficiency in answer correctness, evidence coverage, and precise dual-modal localization, respectively. Doubao-Seed-2.1-Lite achieves the best cost efficiency on all three metrics, at $0.0188, $0.0208, and $0.0491, respectively, with total cost of $13.71. Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash has the lowest total cost ($11.54) and ranks second on all three metrics, at $0.0193, $0.0246, and $0.0780. Gemini3.7-Flash achieves the highest Overall scores among these models on all three metrics, but ranks fourth in each corresponding cost-efficiency column, at $0.0545, $0.0611, and $0.1232. Nevertheless, it outperforms Gemini2.5-Pro across all three metrics while reducing total cost from $224.48 to $44.41 and lowering the respective costs per unit of normalized score by 82.3%, 82.8%, and 83.7%. These results show that stronger performance does not necessarily require higher spending or imply better cost efficiency. Model selection should jointly consider the budget and the required levels of answer correctness, evidence coverage, and localization precision. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce EvaOmni, new evidence-grounded benchmark for audio-visual reasoning. Rather than evaluating only whether model selects the correct answer, EvaOmni also requires the model to identify the supporting evidence necessary to justify its prediction. Through series of rigorous annotation and qualitycontrol procedures, EvaOmni comprises 1,027 questions organized into three hierarchical levels, providing diverse scenarios and rich data for comprehensive evaluation. We further introduce multiple Grounded Score metrics to evaluate the accuracy of evidence localization. Among them, the Coverage Grounded Score rewards 10 evidence coverage, while the Bottleneck Grounded Score prevents strong localization in one modality from masking failure in the other. Additional Grounded Score variants are provided in the Appendix. Large-scale evaluation shows that combining grounded evaluation with accuracy reveals insights missed by accuracy alone. EvaOmni provides reproducible, interpretable basis for measuring progress and identifies precise temporal grounding as the capability current Omni LLMs most clearly lack. We have fully released the data, annotations, and evaluation framework, and we hope they will serve as valuable resource for the research community to advance the development of Omni LLMs.

sections.title: A Dataset Construction and Annotation Details
A Dataset Construction and Annotation Details
sections.content: A.1 Video Collection and Filtering We select candidate videos according to four criteria, aiming to reduce potential training data contamination and textual shortcuts while providing sufficient cues for constructing audio-visual reasoning questions. Temporal freshness and potential contamination screening. We consider only videos uploaded after January 2025. As an additional screening step, we randomly sample three frames from each video and provide them to Gemini3.1-Pro-Preview, asking it to describe the video content. Videos for which the model can reconstruct the full content from these frames are flagged as potential contamination risks and excluded from the candidate pool. This procedure is heuristic: neither the upload date nor the models ability to reconstruct the content establishes whether video was present in its training data. Avoiding subtitle-based textual shortcuts. We exclude videos with hard-coded subtitles to prevent models from substituting on-screen text recognition for audio understanding. This criterion supports the intended requirement that questions depend jointly on audio and visual information. Manageable video duration. We select videos lasting 112 minutes to balance temporal scope, model input budgets, and annotation feasibility. At sampling rate of 1.0 FPS, this range corresponds to approximately 60720 frames, helping control the visual input size while retaining temporally structured event sequences. Extending the collection to longer videos is direction for future work on audio-visual reasoning over longer time spans. Sufficient diversity of entities and events. We prioritize videos with varied participants, actions, or event developments. Videos with highly repetitive content, such as single person continuously performing one action, may provide too few cues for constructing plausible distractors. We manually exclude videos that do not support adequate distractor construction, reducing opportunities to answer questions through unimodal cues or simple elimination. A.2 Annotation Principles and Schema Five senior PhD students with research backgrounds in computer science and specialized knowledge of linguistics participate in annotation. Each sample records the video URL, question, answer options, capability level, and fine-grained capability category. Annotators separately mark the visual and audio evidence supporting the answer, with each evidence segment containing start and end timestamps in mm:ss format and content description. For Level 3 multi-hop reasoning questions, the annotation additionally includes step-by-step reasoning chain. Question and distractor design. Each question must match its assigned capability category and level and be designed to require joint use of audio and visual information. Distractors draw on visual and audio cues present in the video so that single modality is insufficient to reliably distinguish the correct option from the alternatives. They also represent logically plausible alternative explanations, limiting opportunities to eliminate incorrect options solely through wording or logical cues in the question and answer choices. A.3 Human Cross-Validation After initial annotation, each experts question-answer pairs are randomly divided into four parts, which are randomly assigned, one to each of the other four experts, for cross-validation. Each expert therefore reviews approximately as many pairs as they initially annotated. The reviewer checks three dimensions: 1. Capability alignment: whether the question matches its assigned fine-grained capability and capability level. 2. Shortcut susceptibility: whether the question can be reliably answered using only the question and options, audio alone, or vision alone through logical or unimodal cues. 3. Evidence quality: whether the audio and visual evidence intervals and descriptions are accurate and support the annotated answer. Approximately 78% of the initially submitted pairs pass this first review. The remaining disputed pairs are independently reviewed by two additional experts, neither of whom is the original annotator or the first reviewer. pair is discarded if either additional expert identifies problem; it passes only if both approve it. Overall, approximately 82% of the initially submitted pairs pass human cross-validation, while the remaining 18% are discarded at this stage. A.4 Model-Assisted Shortcut Screening Following human validation, we use Gemini3.1-Pro-Preview and Qwen3-Omni-Instruct-30B-A3B for additional shortcut screening under text-only, audio-only, and vision-only conditions. We inspect both the answers and their supporting rationales, as well as the evidence from the available modality in unimodal settings. If model can reliably answer question correctly and provide plausible supporting rationale despite the absence of one or both modalities, the sample is returned for revision. Revised samples must pass model-assisted screening again before inclusion. The resulting EvaOmni benchmark contains 1,027 question-answer pairs curated through this annotation and quality-control process. A.5 EvaOmni Structure EvaOmni contains 392 videos and 1,027 question-answer pairs across three capability levels. The main text defines the three levels; here we define the fine-grained capabilities within each one. Level 1 (436 questions). 1. Temporal Alignment (165 questions): Identify the main content of one modality using information from the other modality. 2. Event Binding (143 questions): Summarize the main event in one modality using information from the other modality. 3. Entity Binding (128 questions): Link the main content of one modality to the corresponding content in the other modality. Level 2 (438 questions). 1. Causal Reasoning (127 questions): Infer the causes of events. 2. Emotional Intelligence (87 questions): Interpret emotional states from audio-visual cues. 3. Intent Understanding (56 questions): Infer persons intent from audio-visual cues. 4. Atmosphere Understanding (28 questions): Interpret the atmosphere of scene from audio-visual cues. 5. Implicit Event Reasoning (18 questions): Infer unstated events, such as an omitted or likely future event. 6. Semantic Disambiguation (30 questions): Resolve the specific meaning of ambiguous speech or behavior using context from both modalities. 7. Temporal Understanding (31 questions): Determine the order, overlap, or duration relationships between audio and visual events. 8. Spatial Understanding (30 questions): Reason about spatial locations and relationships. 9. Conditional Counting (31 questions): Count entities or events that satisfy specified conditions. Level 3 (153 questions). 1. Multi-hop Reasoning (83 questions): Answer questions that require multiple linked inference steps. 2. Long-range Reasoning (35 questions): Integrate dispersed evidence whose most widely separated start times are at least four minutes apart. 3. Multi-Evidence Chain (35 questions): Reason over at least five temporally separated pieces of evidence.

sections.title: Input Preprocessing and Inference Setup
sections.content: Input preprocessing. For evaluation, all videos are resized to 480 pixels on the longer side while preserving their original aspect ratios. Frames are uniformly sampled at 1.0 FPS and provided to the Omni LLMs together with the corresponding audio. For the 112-minute videos in EvaOmni, this configuration keeps the audio-visual inputs within the context windows of the evaluated models. Inference setup. All open-weight models except those in the MiMo family are evaluated on single server equipped with eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, using the inference frameworks and parameter settings recommended in their respective model cards. The three MiMo models are evaluated through MiMos official API platform with the same input preprocessing settings described above. Since the weights of these three models have been publicly released, we classify them as open-weight models. 16 B.2 Human Expert Baseline The human expert baseline is obtained from test participants who are independent of the annotators who constructed the questions and marked the reference evidence. They answer the same questions using the same test videos as the models and report supporting audio and visual intervals; their responses are scored using the same Acc., C.G., and B.G. metrics. Participants may pause and replay the videos when answering and locating evidence. This allowance helps compensate for human memory, which is much more limited than models access to the supplied video context, but it also makes the viewing protocol different from model inference. Even with replay, the need to retain and revisit details across video may disadvantage humans, especially for long or temporally dispersed evidence. We therefore treat the human scores as reference baseline rather than strictly matched comparison of memory or viewing conditions.

Among the updated open-weight models, MiMo-V2.5 obtains the highest overall Mean at 26.3%, trailing Gemini3.7-Flash by 17.4 percentage points. Thus, substantial gap between the leading open-weight and proprietary models persists when the weaker-modality IoU used in B.G. is replaced by average IoU. Performance across capability levels. Mean decreases from Level 1 to Level 2 and again to Level 3 for all 20 models. For example, Gemini3.7-Flash scores 57.0%, 37.6%, and 23.5% across the three levels, while MiMo-V2.5 scores 37.2%, 20.9%, and 10.5%. This pattern is consistent with the greater demands on evidence integration and temporal localization at higher levels. Level 3 remains challenging even when localization quality can be traded off across modalities. Because these scores also incorporate answer correctness, however, the decline cannot be attributed entirely to localization errors. Sensitivity to localization thresholds. Stricter average-IoU thresholds substantially reduce scores. Gemini3.7Flash obtains overall scores of 63.7%, 49.9%, and 26.8% at thresholds of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, respectively; the corresponding scores for MiMo-V2.5 are 39.4%, 27.0%, and 13.6%. Thus, many correctly answered samples satisfying permissive localization criterion fail to meet stricter one. Rankings also depend on the threshold: Gemini3.7-Flash leads in overall Mean, Thr@0.3, and Thr@0.5, whereas Gemini3.8-Flash has slightly higher Thr@0.7 score (27.8% versus 26.8%). Continuous scores and results at multiple thresholds therefore provide complementary information about average performance and success under stricter localization requirements. Ground-truth evidence is read from the annotation file for every model. For each modality, we compute temporal IoU between the unions of the predicted and annotated intervals, without multiplying by answer correctness. Failed inference, response parsing, or truncated output receives zero answer and localization scores and remains in the denominator. Comma-based decimal timestamps are normalized numerically. These choices preserve common evaluation set without granting localization credit to malformed predictions. Let denote answer correctness and Gτ = [min(IoUaudio, IoUvisual) τ ] denote successful dual-modal localization. Unlike the mean-IoU threshold metric above, this criterion requires each modality to meet the threshold. Table 5 reports the four outcomes at τ = 0.5; each outcome is expressed as percentage of all questions. Modality-specific localization. Six of the seven models in Table 5 obtain higher mean audio than visual IoU overall. Among these six, the difference ranges from 0.7 percentage points for Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus to 3.7 points for Gemini3.5-Flash. Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash shows the opposite pattern, with 27.4% audio IoU and 34.3% visual IoU. Answergrounding disagreement. Across the seven models, 47.8%79.8% of correct answers fail the dual-modal localization criterion at τ = 0.5. For Gemini3.7-Flash, 47.8% of correct answers fail grounding, whereas 12.2% of grounding-passing predictions answer incorrectly. The converse error also occurs in the other models: for MiMo-V2.5, 27.9% of grounding-passing predictions answer incorrectly. These outcomes distinguish temporal localization from answer selection; temporal overlap alone establishes neither semantic understanding nor causal use of the reported evidence. Threshold sensitivity. For Gemini3.7-Flash, the fraction of correct answers for which either audio or visual IoU falls below the grounding threshold is 32.9%, 47.8%, and 78.2% at thresholds of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, respectively. These proportions depend on the threshold and are not direct evidence that correct answers were guessed. Figure 31 Performance across fine-grained capabilities. Lines show answer accuracy (Acc.); solid and hatched bars show Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) and Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.), respectively. All values are percentages. Task abbreviations follow the capability taxonomy in Appendix A.5: Level 1: TA = Temporal Alignment, EvB = Event Binding, EnB = Entity Binding; Level 2: CR = Causal Reasoning, EI = Emotional Intelligence, IU = Intent Understanding, AU = Atmosphere Understanding, IEV = Implicit Event Reasoning, TU = Temporal Understanding, CC = Conditional Counting, SD = Semantic Disambiguation, SU = Spatial Understanding; Level 3: LRR = Long-range Reasoning, MEC = Multi-Evidence Chain, MHR = Multi-hop Reasoning. D.4 Analysis Across Fine-Grained Capabilities Figure 31 compares the two representative models across 15 fine-grained capabilities. On the three Level 1 alignment tasks, Gemini3.7-Flash achieves 82.3%88.8% accuracy and 47.5%49.9% B.G., compared with 60.4%68.8% accuracy and 28.1%34.0% B.G. for MiMo-V2.5. Both models show larger separation between answering and precise grounding on complex tasks. On multi-hop reasoning, Gemini3.7-Flash reaches 80.7% accuracy but only 10.6% B.G., while MiMo-V2.5 reaches 44.6% accuracy and 4.9% B.G.; on multi-evidence chains, the corresponding scores are 82.9%/15.6% and 51.4%/8.2%. These comparisons suggest that selecting an answer is substantially easier for both models than locating the dispersed evidence needed to support it.

sections.title: E Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: E.1 Limitations Dataset coverage. EvaOmni contains 1,027 question-answer pairs drawn from 392 videos lasting 112 minutes with sufficient audio-visual cues. Excluding hard-coded subtitles and prioritizing varied entities and events support the construction of questions requiring both modalities, but also constrain the data distribution. The results therefore do not establish generalization to substantially longer videos, subtitle-rich content, scenes with sparse events, or all linguistic and cultural contexts. The three capability levels characterize different task requirements; they do not guarantee strictly increasing difficulty ordering in answer accuracy across different question sets. E.2 Future Work Broader data and task coverage. Future extensions could include longer videos, wider range of linguistic and cultural contexts, and scenes with sparser audio-visual cues while retaining checks for the necessity of both modalities. Subtitle-rich content would also enable explicit separation of text reading from audio understanding. Broader evaluation of open-ended question answering could test whether the current findings hold without cues from answer options.
